pharm: Competitively inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of hepatic cholesterol synthesis, lowering intracellular cholesterol and up-regulating LDL receptors to increase clearance of LDL-cholesterol from the blood.
quick: 20-80 mg/day; 80 mg as extended-release once daily or 40 mg capsule twice daily
May be taken with or without food; often in the evening
Contraindicated - do not breastfeed during therapy
Use caution and do not exceed 40 mg/day in severe renal impairment
Contraindicated in active liver disease/unexplained persistent transaminase elevation
Limit alcohol - additive risk of liver injury
Lipid panel, liver enzymes (as indicated), CK if myalgia, glucose/HbA1c
summary: Fluvastatin is an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (statin) used as an adjunct to diet to lower elevated total and LDL cholesterol, apolipoprotein B and triglycerides and raise HDL in primary hyperlipidemia and mixed dyslipidemia, to slow progression of coronary atherosclerosis, to reduce the risk of coronary revascularization after percutaneous coronary intervention, and to treat heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia in adolescents. The dose range is 20-80 mg daily, given as an 80 mg extended-release tablet once daily or 40 mg capsules once or twice daily. It is contraindicated in active liver disease, pregnancy and breastfeeding. The main adverse effects are myopathy/rhabdomyolysis (risk increased by interacting drugs and higher doses) and transaminase elevations; a small increase in blood glucose/HbA1c can occur. Fluvastatin is the least dependent of the statins on CYP3A4 (metabolized mainly by CYP2C9), so it has fewer CYP3A4-mediated interactions.
indications: Adjunct to diet to reduce elevated total-C, LDL-C, apolipoprotein B and triglycerides and to increase HDL-C in primary hyperlipidemia and mixed dyslipidemia (Fredrickson types IIa and IIb)
Treatment of heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia in adolescent boys and post-menarchal girls (10-16 years)
Slowing progression of coronary atherosclerosis in patients with coronary heart disease
Reduction of the risk of coronary revascularization procedures in patients with coronary heart disease following percutaneous coronary intervention

May be taken with or without food; immediate-release capsules are often taken in the evening, the extended-release tablet at any consistent time
Swallow capsules and extended-release tablets whole
Obtain a baseline lipid panel and assess for secondary causes of dyslipidemia; check liver enzymes if clinically indicated
Advise patients to report promptly any unexplained muscle pain, tenderness or weakness, especially with fever or malaise
Counsel women of childbearing potential to use contraception and stop the drug if pregnancy is planned or occurs
moa: Fluvastatin is a competitive inhibitor of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl coenzyme A (HMG-CoA) reductase, the enzyme catalyzing the rate-limiting step in the conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, an early precursor of cholesterol. By reducing hepatic cholesterol synthesis it depletes intracellular cholesterol, which up-regulates cell-surface LDL receptors and increases hepatic uptake and clearance of circulating LDL-cholesterol. The net effect is reduced plasma total and LDL cholesterol, apolipoprotein B and triglycerides, with a modest rise in HDL cholesterol. Fluvastatin is largely hepatically extracted and metabolized predominantly by CYP2C9.

absolute: Active liver disease or unexplained persistent elevations of serum transaminases
Pregnancy (and women who may become pregnant)
Known hypersensitivity to fluvastatin or any component
relative: Conditions predisposing to myopathy/rhabdomyolysis (renal impairment, hypothyroidism, advanced age, high doses, prior statin myopathy)
Concomitant drugs that increase myopathy risk (fibrates, niacin, cyclosporine, certain antifungals)
Heavy alcohol use or history of liver disease
Predisposition to diabetes (small risk of new-onset diabetes)
monitor: Liver transaminases at baseline and if clinically indicated
Creatine kinase if muscle symptoms occur
Symptoms of myopathy (muscle pain, tenderness, weakness)

preg: Fluvastatin is contraindicated in pregnancy. Cholesterol and products of cholesterol biosynthesis are essential for fetal development, and statins reduce their synthesis; there is no benefit of lipid-lowering during pregnancy. If a patient becomes pregnant while taking fluvastatin, discontinue the drug and advise her of the potential hazard to the fetus.
lact: Fluvastatin is contraindicated during breastfeeding. Because statins are excreted in breast milk (a small amount of fluvastatin appears in human milk) and could disrupt infant lipid metabolism, women requiring fluvastatin should not breastfeed.
renal: Fluvastatin is largely metabolized by the liver with little renal excretion of unchanged drug, so mild-to-moderate renal impairment needs no major adjustment. In severe renal impairment, use with caution and do not exceed 40 mg/day, as higher doses have not been adequately studied; renal impairment also increases myopathy risk.
hepatic: Fluvastatin is contraindicated in active liver disease or unexplained persistent transaminase elevations. It can cause dose-related, usually reversible transaminase increases; obtain liver enzyme tests before starting and as clinically indicated, and discontinue if transaminase elevations are persistent and exceed three times the upper limit of normal or if clinical liver injury occurs.

major: Cyclosporine - markedly increases fluvastatin exposure and myopathy risk; limit fluvastatin dose (do not exceed 20 mg twice daily)
Fibrates (especially gemfibrozil) - increased risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis
moderate: Fluconazole and other CYP2C9 inhibitors - increase fluvastatin levels
Warfarin - fluvastatin may potentiate anticoagulant effect; monitor INR when starting or changing dose
Phenytoin - mutual increases in plasma levels; monitor
Rifampin - induces metabolism and lowers fluvastatin levels
minor: Cholestyramine - reduces absorption; separate dosing by at least 4 hours
Cimetidine, ranitidine, omeprazole - small increases in fluvastatin levels
interactions.food: Food slows absorption rate but does not reduce overall effect; may be taken with or without food.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol intake; heavy use increases the risk of hepatotoxicity.
interactions.diagnostics: May elevate liver transaminases and creatine kinase; can modestly raise fasting glucose/HbA1c.

serious: Myopathy and rhabdomyolysis (with possible acute renal failure)
Immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (rare, persists after stopping)
rare: Hypersensitivity reactions including angioedema and anaphylaxis
Cognitive complaints (memory loss, confusion, usually reversible)
emergency: Rhabdomyolysis (severe muscle pain/weakness with dark urine and renal impairment)
Acute hepatic injury (jaundice, severe abdominal pain)

monitoring: Fasting lipid panel before and after starting/changing therapy (efficacy)
Liver transaminases at baseline and when clinically indicated; investigate persistent elevations
Creatine kinase if unexplained muscle pain, tenderness or weakness occurs
Renal function if rhabdomyolysis is suspected
counsel: Take this medicine regularly along with a low-cholesterol, heart-healthy diet
Report promptly any unexplained muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness, especially with fever or dark urine
Tell your doctor if you have yellowing of the skin or eyes, unusual tiredness, or severe stomach pain (signs of liver problems)
Do not take this medicine if you are pregnant, planning pregnancy, or breastfeeding - use reliable contraception
Limit alcohol and tell your doctor about all other medicines, especially other cholesterol drugs and certain antibiotics/antifungals
Keep your blood-test and clinic appointments to check cholesterol, and liver/muscle tests if needed
pk: LDL reduction begins within days; maximal lipid effect within ~4 weeks
Immediate-release Tmax <1 hour; extended-release Tmax ~3 hours
Lipid-lowering effect maintained with once-daily dosing
Store at 25 C (excursions 15-30 C); protect from light and moisture
pearls: Contraindicated in pregnancy, breastfeeding and active liver disease - stop if a patient becomes pregnant
Fluvastatin is metabolized mainly by CYP2C9 (least CYP3A4-dependent statin), so it has fewer CYP3A4 interactions than simvastatin/atorvastatin
Myopathy/rhabdomyolysis risk rises with higher doses and with fibrates, niacin, cyclosporine, and colchicine - measure CK for muscle symptoms
Statins can cause a small increase in blood glucose/HbA1c (new-onset diabetes) - benefit still outweighs this risk in most patients
Separate from bile-acid sequestrants (cholestyramine) by at least 4 hours to preserve absorption
Monitor INR when starting or stopping in patients on warfarin
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at once.
overdose: There is no specific treatment for fluvastatin overdose. Symptoms are usually limited; management is supportive with monitoring of liver function and creatine kinase. Because fluvastatin is highly protein-bound, hemodialysis is not expected to enhance its clearance. Treat any rhabdomyolysis with aggressive hydration and supportive care.
